analysis.one_liner: Lets college athletes unionize and collectively bargain over pay and working conditions.
analysis.headline: Introduced with one cosponsor, the bill was referred to the Senate labor committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal labor law so that college athletes who receive scholarships or other compensation tied to playing a sport count as employees with the right to form unions and bargain collectively. It would cover public universities for this purpose, let athletes at schools in the same athletic conference bargain together as one unit, and bar schools from making athletes sign away that right in scholarship agreements. The National Labor Relations Board would enforce these rights.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes who receive any direct compensation from their school tied to playing an intercollegiate sport — including scholarship ("grant-in-aid") recipients — would become employees under the National Labor Relations Act. They could form or join unions, bargain with their schools and, if they choose, with their whole athletic conference as one unit, and could not be made to waive those rights in scholarship agreements [S3]. The bill's findings note that intercollegiate sports generate more than $15 billion a year and that athletes have no say over the rules that govern their compensation, health, and safety [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Defines college athletes as employees of their schools if they receive direct compensation, including scholarships, whose terms require them to play a sport — giving them standing to organize and bargain under federal labor law [S3].

Covers public universities, which the National Labor Relations Act normally does not reach, so athletes at state schools — the majority of big-time college sports — get the same rights as athletes at private schools [S3].

Lets the NLRB treat all schools in an athletic conference as one bargaining unit if the athletes' representatives consent, mirroring how professional athletes bargain league-wide with team owners [S3].
Bars schools from using scholarship agreements or settlements to waive these rights, so athletes cannot be forced to give up organizing as a condition of aid [S3].
Keeps the change from altering athletes' tax treatment or their eligibility for federal financial aid like Pell Grants, so organizing would not cost them aid dollars [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Universities and athletic conferences, which would lose the power to set athlete compensation and conditions unilaterally. The NCAA and member schools currently cap compensation and control athletes' terms through scholarship agreements; collective bargaining would shift money and negotiating leverage to athletes, to be worked out in contracts with athletic departments [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill extends federal labor law to public universities, which have historically been outside the National Labor Relations Act; that is a major change in how states' own colleges manage their workforces and would inevitably face constitutional and state-authority challenges, which the severability clause acknowledges by trying to keep the rest of the bill alive if parts fall [S3].

Bargaining at the conference level would spread uniform contract terms across very different institutions — small private schools and large public flagships in the same conference — which schools could argue does not fit their varying budgets [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that whatever athletes win at the bargaining table — more compensation, better medical protections — comes out of athletic-department budgets and conference revenues, and schools would fight the classification of athletes as employees rather than accept it voluntarily [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs to tens of thousands of scholarship athletes, many from modest backgrounds, who would gain the same collective-bargaining rights professional athletes used to end exploitative practices [S3]. The cost falls on universities and the NCAA, concentrated in athletic departments and conference revenues. The bill is drafted carefully — it protects athletes' tax treatment and financial-aid eligibility, excludes the NCAA itself from the conference bargaining-unit definition, and requires athlete consent before a conference-wide unit forms [S3] — but its core premise, extending federal labor law to public universities, was certain to draw years of litigation. The central obstacle was not design but that it never moved at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and nothing further ever happened to it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Murphy introduced the bill on May 27, 2021, with Senator Bernie Sanders as the original cosponsor; it was read twice and referred to the HELP Committee the same day [S1][S3][S5].
The HELP Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S5].
The bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with only one cosponsor and no committee action in its entire run [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The NCAA and its member institutions are better off because the bill died: they keep their ability to cap athlete compensation and set conditions through scholarship agreements without facing unionized athletes across a conference. The status quo also saves universities from a major new labor-law obligation.

for.name: Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it as lead sponsor; no committee action followed his referral request.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee where the bill sat, never scheduled a hearing or markup on it in the roughly 19 months before the Congress ended.

against.name: NCAA and its member institutions
against.role: Governing body of college sports and its 1,100+ schools
against.what_they_did: The bill names the NCAA as the entity whose rules cap athlete compensation and define athletes as amateurs; NCAA members benefit from the bill's failure, and the association has long opposed employee status for college athletes.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape is unknown; the only recorded support came from two progressive senators, one Democrat and one Independent, and no Republican cosponsored [S3][S4].

industries.industry: NCAA and college sports governing bodies
industries.note: The bill's findings describe the NCAA as colluding with member schools to cap athlete compensation and control athletes' labor under an 'amateur' label [S3]. Unionized athletes bargaining conference-wide would take away the NCAA's unilateral control over pay and conditions, which is why the bill pointedly defines athletic conferences to exclude the NCAA from the bargaining table [S3].

The bill makes public universities 'employers' of their college athletes under federal labor law, ending their exemption from the National Labor Relations Act for this workforce [S3]. Whatever athletes won in bargaining — more compensation, medical and safety protections — would come from athletic-department budgets.

Private schools already fall under the NLRB, but the bill explicitly extends jurisdiction to them in the context of intercollegiate athletics and lets athletes bargain across a whole conference, expanding what they could face at the table [S3].
